clinicalPearls: An autoinflammatory bone disease producing sterile, often multifocal osteomyelitis, with the recurrent multifocal form termed CRMO
Presents with insidious bone pain, local swelling and sometimes low-grade fever, frequently affecting the metaphyses of long bones, clavicle, spine and pelvis
Clavicular involvement is a characteristic clue, and the sternoclavicular region may be affected
It is a diagnosis of exclusion; cultures are negative and there is no response to antibiotics, which helps distinguish it from bacterial osteomyelitis
Whole-body MRI is valuable for detecting clinically silent lesions and defining the full extent of disease
Associations include psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and palmoplantar pustulosis (within the SAPHO spectrum in older patients)
Treatment uses NSAIDs first line, with bisphosphonates (particularly for vertebral disease), TNF inhibition or other agents for refractory or spinal involvement
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis is an autoinflammatory disorder in which dysregulated innate immunity produces sterile inflammation of bone. An imbalance between proinflammatory cytokines and inadequate anti-inflammatory signalling, with activation of the inflammasome and osteoclast-driven bone remodelling, leads to osteitis, bone oedema, lytic and sclerotic change and, in the spine, vertebral collapse. The absence of an infective organism and the frequent overlap with other autoinflammatory and immune-mediated conditions such as psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease underline its immune-mediated basis.
additionalDifferentials: Malignancy such as leukaemia, Ewing sarcoma, osteosarcoma or metastatic neuroblastoma
additionalInvestigations: Whole-body MRI to identify multifocal and clinically silent lesions
Inflammatory markers, which may be normal or only mildly raised
Blood cultures and, where needed, bone biopsy with culture to exclude infection and malignancy
Plain radiographs showing mixed lytic and sclerotic change
Bone biopsy histology when malignancy cannot otherwise be excluded
Screening for associated psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease
Spinal imaging to detect vertebral involvement
redFlags: Vertebral involvement with risk of collapse and spinal deformity
Features suggesting malignancy such as an aggressive lesion, night pain or systemic upset
High fever and systemic toxicity suggesting genuine infection
reference.prognosis: The course is variable, ranging from a single self-limiting episode to a chronic relapsing disease over years. Most children do well with treatment, but vertebral involvement can cause permanent deformity, and some have persistent or recurrent symptoms into adulthood.
pitfalls: Treating repeatedly for presumed bacterial osteomyelitis despite negative cultures and no antibiotic response
Failing to perform whole-body MRI and thereby underestimating disease extent
Missing vertebral disease and the risk of collapse
Not excluding malignancy before settling on the diagnosis
Overlooking associated skin and bowel disease
references: Consensus recommendations for CNO/CRMO diagnosis and management
PRINTO/PReS guidance on autoinflammatory bone disease
management: First-line non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to suppress the sterile bone inflammation and control pain
Bisphosphonates (such as pamidronate) for refractory disease and especially vertebral involvement to limit collapse and remodelling
Escalation to TNF-alpha inhibitors or conventional DMARDs such as methotrexate or sulfasalazine, with corticosteroids, for disease unresponsive to NSAIDs
Whole-body MRI surveillance to detect clinically silent lesions and monitor disease extent
Screening for and management of associated psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and palmoplantar pustulosis
Physiotherapy and multimodal pain management to preserve function
Paediatric rheumatology-led multidisciplinary care with monitoring for spinal deformity
